--- title: "DATA100 Introduction to Data Analysis" subtitle: "Lecture 3: The Whole Game - Day 2" author: "Agassi Iu" institute: "Wilfrid Laurier University" date: "September 17, 2026" format: live-revealjs: resources: - data/raw_survey_2017.csv - data/raw_survey_2022.csv theme: sky slide-number: true transition: slide incremental: true embed-resources: true # Embeds figures and libraries into a single portable HTML file filters: - live execute: echo: true warning: false # Hides warnings and package loading messages message: false --- ## Recap: Day 1 - We toured real findings — income, benefits, paycheque-delay difficulty - We ended with three financial wellness clusters: Stressed, Coping, Comfortable - Today: how we actually got there — including the messy parts --- ## Before we look at the raw data...
What do you think could go wrong with real, raw survey data?

What kinds of problems might it have that yesterday's polished plots didn't show?
--- ## The reveal: here's the actual raw file ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) survey_2017_raw <- read_csv("data/raw_survey_2017.csv") # Note the skip = 1 -- 2022's file has a stray metadata line above the # real header (a leftover from the export on the new survey platform) survey_2022_raw <- read_csv("data/raw_survey_2022.csv", skip = 1) glimpse(survey_2017_raw) glimpse(survey_2022_raw) ``` ::: --- ## First things first: duplicate rows A few respondents show up more than once (simulating a double-submitted survey). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_raw |> count(respondent_id, sort = TRUE) |> filter(n > 1) survey_2017_raw <- survey_2017_raw |> distinct() survey_2022_raw <- survey_2022_raw |> distinct() ``` ::: `distinct()` removes exact duplicate rows — simple, but always worth checking for *before* anything else, since duplicates quietly inflate every count and mean you compute downstream. --- ## Tidy data: benefits are stuck in wide format ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_raw |> select(respondent_id, starts_with("benefit_")) |> head() ``` ::: One respondent, one true preference — but it's spread across six columns. This needs `pivot_longer()` before we can do anything useful with it. --- ## Tidy data: `pivot_longer()` to the rescue ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} benefits_2017_long <- survey_2017_raw |> pivot_longer( cols = starts_with("benefit_"), names_to = "benefit_type", values_to = "response" ) |> mutate(chosen = response %in% c("Yes", "Y", "yes")) |> group_by(respondent_id) |> summarize( benefit_preference = if (any(chosen)) benefit_type[chosen][1] else NA_character_, .groups = "drop" ) survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_raw |> select(-starts_with("benefit_")) |> left_join(benefits_2017_long, by = "respondent_id") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} benefits_2022_long <- survey_2022_raw |> pivot_longer( cols = starts_with("benefit_"), names_to = "benefit_type", values_to = "response" ) |> mutate(chosen = response %in% c("Yes", "Y", "yes")) |> group_by(respondent_id) |> summarize( benefit_preference = if (any(chosen)) benefit_type[chosen][1] else NA_character_, .groups = "drop" ) survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_raw |> select(-starts_with("benefit_")) |> left_join(benefits_2022_long, by = "respondent_id") ``` ::: --- ## Strings & expressions: income is a mess ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean |> distinct(income) |> slice_sample(n = 6) ``` ::: Four different formats mixed together: `"85000"`, `"$85,000"`, `"85,000"`, `"85K"`. Before income can be used in any calculation, it needs to become a real number. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean_income <- function(x) { x <- str_trim(x) is_k <- str_detect(x, "K$") numeric_part <- x |> str_remove_all("[$,K]") |> as.numeric() if_else(is_k, numeric_part * 1000, numeric_part) } survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(income = clean_income(income)) survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(income = clean_income(income)) ``` ::: --- ## Strings & expressions: province spelling ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean |> distinct(province) ``` ::: Same province, several spellings: `"Ontario"`, `"ON"`, `"ontario "`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} standardize_province <- function(x) { x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower() case_when( x %in% c("ontario", "on") ~ "Ontario", x %in% c("alberta", "ab") ~ "Alberta", x %in% c("british columbia", "bc") ~ "British Columbia", x %in% c("quebec", "qc") ~ "Quebec", TRUE ~ str_to_title(x) ) } survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province)) survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(province = standardize_province(province)) ``` ::: --- ## Strings & expressions: Yes/No encodings ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean |> distinct(debt_overwhelmed) ``` ::: Three encodings for the same two answers: `"Yes"/"No"`, `"Y"/"N"`, `"yes"/"no"`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} standardize_yn <- function(x) { x <- str_trim(x) |> str_to_lower() case_when( x %in% c("yes", "y") ~ "Yes", x %in% c("no", "n") ~ "No", TRUE ~ NA_character_ ) } survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed)) survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(debt_overwhelmed = standardize_yn(debt_overwhelmed)) ``` ::: --- ## Missing data: how much, and where? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean |> summarize(across(everything(), ~ mean(is.na(.)))) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "pct_missing") |> arrange(desc(pct_missing)) ``` ::: --- ## Missing data: two honest options ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="48%"} **Option 1: Delete** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_nomiss <- survey_2017_clean |> drop_na(income, savings_pct, debt_overwhelmed, emergency_fund_likelihood) ``` ::: Simple, but shrinks your sample — and if missingness isn't random, you bias what's left. ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} **Option 2: Impute** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_imputed <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(savings_pct = if_else( is.na(savings_pct), median(savings_pct, na.rm = TRUE), savings_pct )) ``` ::: Keeps every row, but every imputed value is a guess — and a bad guess can quietly distort your results. ::: ::: --- ## Mismatched response: too many response levels ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean |> distinct(emergency_fund_likelihood) survey_2022_clean |> distinct(emergency_fund_likelihood) ``` ::: 2017 has 7 levels. 2022 already collapsed to 5. Neither matches the other, and neither is easy to compare across years as-is. **The compromise:** collapse both down to 3 levels — Difficult, Neither, Manageable. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when( emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult", "Somewhat difficult") ~ "Difficult", emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither", emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Somewhat manageable", "Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable", TRUE ~ NA_character_ )) survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> mutate(emergency_fund_3lvl = case_when( emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Very difficult", "Difficult") ~ "Difficult", emergency_fund_likelihood == "Neither" ~ "Neither", emergency_fund_likelihood %in% c("Manageable", "Very manageable") ~ "Manageable", TRUE ~ NA_character_ )) ``` ::: --- ## Mismatched question: same question, different name ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(survey_2017_clean) names(survey_2022_clean) ``` ::: `paycheque_delay_difficulty` (2017) and `twoweek_pay_delay_impact` (2022) ask the same thing — the survey platform changed, the wording changed, the column name changed. `rename()` fixes this in one line each. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> rename(pay_delay_response = paycheque_delay_difficulty) survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> rename(pay_delay_response = twoweek_pay_delay_impact) ``` ::: --- ## Age: numbers in one year, buckets in the other ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean |> select(age) |> head() survey_2022_clean |> select(age) |> head() ``` ::: 2017 gives an exact age. 2022 gives a bracket. To compare years, everyone needs to speak the same bucket language. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(age_bucket = case_when( age <= 30 ~ "18-30", age <= 40 ~ "30-40", age <= 50 ~ "40-50", age <= 65 ~ "50-65", TRUE ~ "65+" )) survey_2022_clean <- survey_2022_clean |> rename(age_bucket = age) ``` ::: --- ## Removed benefit option: aligning categories ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean |> distinct(benefit_preference) survey_2022_clean |> distinct(benefit_preference) ``` ::: "Educational funding" existed as a choice in 2017, but the 2022 platform dropped it. To compare years fairly, we fold anything not offered in both years into a shared **"Other"** category. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_2017_clean <- survey_2017_clean |> mutate(benefit_preference = if_else( benefit_preference == "benefit_education", "benefit_other", benefit_preference )) ``` ::: --- ## Combine years ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_combined <- bind_rows(survey_2017_clean, survey_2022_clean) glimpse(survey_combined) ``` ::: Only possible now — column names match (`rename()`), category sets match (the "Other" recode), and the response scales match (the 3-level collapse). Every fix so far existed to make this one line possible. --- ## A useful side quest: `separate()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_combined |> separate(respondent_id, into = c("survey_year", "respondent_num"), sep = "-") |> select(survey_year, respondent_num, everything()) |> head() ``` ::: `respondent_id` (`"2017-0001"`) is actually two pieces of information squeezed into one column. `separate()` is `pivot_longer()`'s cousin for this specific problem — splitting one messy column into several clean ones. --- ## `pivot_wider()`: the mirror image ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_combined |> count(financial_wellness_cluster, year) |> pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = n) ``` ::: `pivot_longer()` took wide data and made it long. `pivot_wider()` does the opposite — useful here for turning a long count table into a clean side-by-side year comparison, exactly the shape you'd want for a report. --- ## Show concluding results ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey_combined |> ggplot(aes(x = financial_wellness_cluster, y = income, fill = factor(year))) + geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8)) + labs(title = "Income by Cluster: 2017 vs 2022", x = "Cluster", y = "Income ($)", fill = "Year") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: This is the exact plot style from Day 1 — except now you've watched every step of how the data underneath it got here. --- ## Back to your predictions
Which of your guesses from the start of class came true?

What did we run into that nobody predicted?
--- ## A few honest cautions - Every cleaning choice was also an analytical choice — a different 3-level collapse, a different age-bucket rule, a different imputation method could all shift what we find downstream - This dataset is synthetic — today's numbers are illustrative, not a claim about real Canadians - Later this semester: missing-data methods and statistical tests that let you make these calls more rigorously than by eyeballing

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
